document_check.note: Robbins CB, Grewal DS, Thompson AC, et al. Choroidal Structural Analysis in Alzheimer Disease, Mild Cognitive Impairment, and Cognitively Healthy Controls. Am J Ophthalmol 2021;223:359-367. This is a prospective cross-sectional study with 74 MCI patients (143 eyes) and 137 controls (248 eyes). Multivariable GEE shows no MCI versus control difference in SFCT (p = .599) and lower CVI in MCI (p = .002). The authors and findings match the cited sentence.

cited_result: Multivariable GEE comparison of subfoveal choroidal thickness between MCI (143 eyes, 74 participants) and cognitively healthy controls (248 eyes, 137 participants), adjusted for age, sex and logMAR visual acuity: no significant difference (p = .599), whereas the choroidal vascularity index was lower in MCI (p = .002).
tool_reason: The cited result is a between-group comparison of an imaging biomarker (SFCT) in MCI against controls measured at one time point. For this appraisal the exposure is diagnostic group (item 3), the condition criteria are item 4, and the outcome is the choroidal measurement (item 7).

domains.domain: 1. Were the criteria for inclusion in the sample clearly defined?
domains.rationale: Age threshold, diagnostic confirmation, control definition and ocular and systemic exclusions are stated.

signalling.question: Were the criteria for inclusion in the sample clearly defined?
signalling.quote: Subjects aged 50 years or older with a clinical diagnosis of AD or MCI were enrolled from the Duke Neurological Disorders Clinics. ... All subjects with a known history of non-AD dementia, diabetes mellitus, glaucoma, retinal pathology, or refractive error

domains.domain: 2. Were the study subjects and the setting described in detail?
domains.rationale: The setting (Duke clinics and a prevention registry) and group demographics are reported (Table 1). The recruitment period and sampling method are not stated.

signalling.question: Were the study subjects and the setting described in detail?
signalling.quote: Healthy volunteers aged 50 years or older without subjective memory impairment or a history of neurologic disease were enrolled from the Duke Neurological Disorders Clinics and the Duke Alzheimer's Disease Prevention Registry of cognitively healthy, community-dwelling volunteers

domains.domain: 3. Was the exposure (diagnostic group) measured in a valid and reliable way?
domains.rationale: MCI was confirmed by a single specialist under NIA-AA guidance. Controls were classified by a different route: absence of subjective complaint and a MoCA score of 23 or more, without the same specialist assessment. The MCI group's MMSE spread (24.45 ± 5.85) is wide, so misclassification in either direction cannot be excluded.

signalling.question: Was the exposure measured in a valid and reliable way?
signalling.quote: Each patient's diagnosis was confirmed before study participation by an experienced memory disorders specialist (A.L.) ... cognitively healthy, community-dwelling volunteers who had a Montreal Cognitive Assessment score of >_23.

domains.domain: 4. Were objective, standard criteria used for measurement of the condition?
domains.rationale: MCI was diagnosed according to NIA-AA recommendations.

signalling.question: Were objective, standard criteria used for measurement of the condition?
signalling.quote: in accordance with diagnostic guidelines and recommendations of the National Institute on Aging-Alzheimer's Association.

domains.rationale: Age, sex and visual acuity were named as confounders, and the authors identify axial length as a determinant of choroidal thickness.

signalling.question: Were confounding factors identified?
signalling.quote: multivariable GEE models were then constructed to adjust for the potential confounders of age, sex, and logMAR VA. ... Because high axial length might influence choroidal thickness measurements, it will be important to obtain axial length values in future work.

domains.domain: 6. Were strategies to deal with confounding factors stated?
domains.rationale: Adjustment for age, sex and visual acuity is stated. Axial length, which the authors themselves name as a determinant of SFCT, was not measured. Refractive error was handled only by excluding participants beyond ±6 D on record or verbal report, so adjustment for the main confounder of the cited outcome is incomplete.

signalling.question: Were strategies to deal with confounding factors stated?
signalling.quote: Axial length measurement was not routinely performed as part of this study because of the absence of an A-scan unit at our primary imaging site (a neurologic disorders clinic).

domains.domain: 7. Were the outcomes measured in a valid and reliable way?
domains.rationale: SFCT was measured on EDI-OCT by two independent masked graders, with averaging, third-grader adjudication and image-quality exclusions.

signalling.question: Were the outcomes measured in a valid and reliable way?
signalling.quote: Two independent, masked graders (B.W.P., J.H.P.) measured the SFCT, and these measurements were averaged to determine the final value. In cases of significant measurement differences between the 2 graders, as defined by a coefficient of variation >5%, a third grader (D.S.G.) adjudicated the SFCT measurement.

domains.rationale: The GEE accounts for the correlation between eyes and adjusts for covariates; confidence intervals are reported.

signalling.question: Was appropriate statistical analysis used?
signalling.quote: using generalized estimating equations (GEEs) to account for the correlation between eyes of the same subject.

overall: Some concerns (JBI: items 3 and 6 unclear; all other items yes)
overall_rationale: No item among confounder identification, confounder strategy, outcome measurement or analysis is answered No. Under the review's rule, the two Unclear items give some concerns: differential ascertainment of controls (item 3) and no measurement or adjustment of axial length, which the authors identify as a determinant of SFCT (item 6). Outcome measurement and analysis are strong.

applicability.rationale: The cases are clinic MCI patients diagnosed clinically without amyloid or CSF confirmation (acknowledged by the authors), which is relevant to clinical MCI.
